quiz.title: IP Quiz
theory.address.binaryNote: The bar sits on the /{prefix} boundary. Left of it are the {prefix} network bits — identical in every row, which is what the AND preserves. Right of it are the {hostBits} host bits, and they are the only difference between the two results: all 0 gives the network address, all 1 gives the broadcast address. Everything in between is a usable host.
theory.hostCount.binaryNote: Only the {hostBits} digits right of the bar can change, and {hostBits} bits have 2^{hostBits} = {total} combinations. Two of them are spoken for — all zeros is the network address, all ones the broadcast address — which leaves {usable}. The address itself never enters the calculation.
theory.split.binaryNote: The {bits} S bits were host bits before the split; borrowing them moved the boundary {bits} places to the right. They simply count up, which is why there are exactly {rounded} subnets and why that octet steps in {step}s.
theory.mask.binaryNote: Count the ones and you have the prefix — {prefix} of them here, and nothing else to a mask. They always come in one run, and everything after them is zeros. The last row breaks that rule: after a zero another one appears, 10100000, so 255.255.255.160 is not a mask at all.
theory.address.worked3: Network value from the host octet
theory.address.thought1: 255 means the whole octet belongs to the network and 0 means the whole octet is free. The one the boundary actually falls in is octet {position}, and that is the one you work with.
theory.address.thought3: The blocks start at {blocks} and so on. You need the last one that is still at or below {octet}: {octet} ÷ {size} = {times}, so the network starts at {times} × {size} = {value}.
theory.address.thought4: The next network starts at {next}, so the last address that still belongs to ours is the one immediately before it. In the octets after it, everything is set to its maximum.
theory.hostCount.thought2: Every one of the {hostBits} bits is independent and can be 0 or 1. Two possibilities for the first, doubled by the second, doubled again by the third, and so on.
theory.hostCount.thought3: These two are not free to hand out: one names the network itself, the other addresses everyone in it at once. Every other combination is a host.
theory.split.thought1: Equally sized subnets only come in powers of two, so count them out until one is big enough for {splits}: that is 2^{bits} = {rounded}. So you make {rounded} subnets and simply leave the {spare} you do not need unused.
theory.split.thought1Exact: Equally sized subnets only come in powers of two, and {splits} already is one: 2^{bits}. Nothing to round up here, and none of the subnets goes to waste.
theory.split.thought2: The exponent is the number of bits: {rounded} subnets came from 2^{bits}, so {bits} of them. Those are exactly the bits you take from the host part.
theory.mask.thought2: The {rest} leftover bits are the leftmost ones of the octet, and the leftmost bits carry the largest values: {values}, which add up to {value}. The shortcut 256 − 2^(8 − r) says the same thing in one step.
theory.address.title: Network and broadcast address
theory.address.intro: Two methods get you there: a binary AND, or the block size. Go binary when the prefix is unfamiliar, use the block size when you want to be quick.
theory.address.step1: Find the interesting octet: the first octet of the mask that is not 255.
theory.address.step2: Block size = 256 − that octet of the mask.
theory.address.step3: The largest multiple of the block size that is less than or equal to the host octet is the network value.
theory.address.step4: The broadcast address is the one address before the next block starts.
theory.address.thought3Edge: The boundary falls exactly on an octet edge here, so one block covers the whole of octet {position}. Every network therefore starts at 0, and each octet to the right of the boundary is 0 in the network address.
theory.address.thought4Edge: The broadcast address is the other way round: right of the boundary everything is at its maximum, so 255.
theory.address.note: Usable hosts = 2^(32 − prefix) − 2; the network and broadcast addresses do not count. In binary you can read it straight off: the network bits stay as they are, host bits all 0 give the network address and all 1 give the broadcast address.
theory.hostCount.title: Usable host addresses
theory.hostCount.intro: The count depends on the prefix alone. Which address the question shows makes no difference to the answer — it only tells you which network you are in.
theory.hostCount.step2: Every combination of those bits is one address, so the network holds 2^host bits addresses.
theory.hostCount.step3: Two of them are taken: all host bits 0 is the network address, all 1 is the broadcast address.
theory.hostCount.note: Only the prefix matters: any address with the same prefix as {subject} has exactly as many usable addresses. The exceptions are /31 (point-to-point, RFC 3021) and /32 (a single host route), where the formula would give 0 and −1.
theory.split.title: Splitting a network into subnets
theory.split.intro: Equally sized subnets only come in powers of two: you borrow bits from the host part, and those bits lengthen the prefix.
theory.split.step1: Round the number of subnets you need up to the next power of two.
theory.split.step2: 2^n is that number, so you borrow n bits.
theory.split.step4: The new networks follow one block size apart, starting at the original network.
theory.split.note: Two common traps: the new networks carry the new prefix (/{new}, not /{old}), and counting starts at the first block — the first subnet is {first}, the second is {second}.
theory.mask.title: Converting between prefix and mask
theory.mask.intro: A valid mask is a run of ones followed by a run of zeros. The prefix counts exactly those ones.
theory.mask.step1: Prefix to mask: every 8 ones make 255. If r bits are left over, that octet is 256 − 2^(8 − r), and the rest is 0.
theory.mask.step2: Mask to prefix: count the ones. Each 255 contributes 8, the interesting octet contributes what the table below shows.
theory.mask.step3: Only these octet values are valid: 255, 254, 252, 248, 240, 224, 192, 128, 0.
theory.mask.note: 255.255.255.160 is invalid: 160 is 10100000 in binary, so the ones are not in one run.
